title: How to Use Social Media: A Guide for Liquor Store Owners
summary: A practical social media guide for liquor stores. Learn which platforms to use, what to post, how to age-gate your accounts, and which alcohol rules apply.
body_markdown:
Social media is the cheapest way for an independent liquor store to show the neighborhood what's on its shelves. A 30-second video of an allocated bourbon coming off the truck can fill the store by noon, and it costs nothing but the time it takes to film it.


According to Pew Research,[71% of U.S. adults use Facebook](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/11/20/americans-social-media-use-2025/) and about half visit it every day, while around 80% of adults aged 18 to 29 use Instagram.


The catch is that alcohol isn't a normal retail category. Platforms restrict who can see your posts and ads, states limit how you can advertise prices and run giveaways, and the brands you carry often can't pay you to promote them.


This guide covers which platforms are worth your time, the rules to know before you post, what to share, and how to turn followers into customers who actually walk through the door.


## Which Social Media Platforms Should a Liquor Store Use?


You don't need to be everywhere. Two platforms run well will do more for you than five you post on once a month.


- **Facebook:** Facebook is where most of your local, over-30 customers spend much of their time. It's the best place to list tastings and events, join neighborhood groups, and collect reviews. If you were to only pick one platform, this is usually it. Age-restrict your page, and set any ads to target 21 and older.
- **Instagram:** Built for what liquor stores do well visually: a new bottle on the shelf, a staff pick, a stacked holiday display. Reels reach people who don't follow you yet, and Stories suit quick updates like "just landed" or "two left." Set a 21+ minimum age on your account.
- **TikTok:** Strongest with younger shoppers, and works best if someone on your team is comfortable on camera. Treat it as organic only: TikTok shows alcohol content only to age-appropriate users and doesn't let retailers run ads that promote alcohol sales or delivery.
- **Vivino, Untappd, and Wine-Searcher:** These are where serious wine and beer shoppers go to look for specific bottles. A Vivino or Wine-Searcher listing can bring in a customer who drove past three other stores for a wine only you carry, and Untappd lets a beer-focused shop show what's on the shelf right now.


Whichever platforms you choose, don't skip your Google Business Profile. It isn't a social network, but it may be the most valuable profile you manage. When someone searches for a liquor store nearby, your photos, hours, reviews, and recent posts appear right in the results, and a weekly update takes only a few minutes.


## What Can Liquor Stores Legally Post on Social Media?


Most social media advice is written for coffee shops and clothing boutiques. Liquor stores, however, have a few extra rules to follow, and breaking them can get your account restricted or draw attention from your state alcohol agency.


Rules vary by state, so treat this as a starting point and confirm the details with your state agency.


Rule How to stay compliant


Age-gate your accounts Instagram and Facebook let business accounts set a minimum age for who can see their content. Set yours to 21 to keep posts away from minors.


Follow each platform’s ad rules Meta allows alcohol ads that follow local law, but its policy only bars targeting people under 18, so set U.S. campaigns to 21+ yourself. TikTok doesn’t let retailers advertise alcohol sales or delivery at all.


Check your state’s advertising rules Some states restrict how retailers advertise prices, discounts, or “free” offers. In[control states](https://www.santehq.com/blog/abc-states-guide-liquor-store-owners) , minimum pricing can make some discount posts illegal even when the checkout price is fine.


Be careful with giveaways Don’t offer alcohol as a prize; use merchandise, glassware, or event tickets instead. Keep entry 21+ with no purchase required, and skip purchase-based raffles for allocated bottles, which can count as illegal lotteries in many states. Some states also require you to register larger sweepstakes.


Watch your brand partnerships Tied-house laws generally stop suppliers and distributors from paying or rewarding you to promote their products, whether with cash, free product, or paid boosts. The[TTB](https://www.ttb.gov/public-information/industry-circulars/ttb-industry-circular-2024-1) also treats a supplier’s likes and reposts of your content as its own advertising.


Keep content responsible Don’t show anyone drinking to excess, anyone who looks under 21, or alcohol near driving. Delete comments that tag minors or encourage heavy drinking, and keep a short written policy for your staff.


Vet local creators Partners should be 21+ with a mostly adult audience. Industry advertising codes set the bar at 73.8% of legal drinking age. Paid posts must be clearly disclosed.


### How to Set Up Your Liquor Store's Social Media Profiles


A good profile answers a new visitor's first questions before they have to ask: where you are, when you're open, and why they should come to you instead of the store down the road.


- **Use the same details everywhere:** Your store name, address, phone number, and hours should match across every platform and your website. Inconsistent details hurt your local search rankings.
- **Keep hours current:** Holiday hours and any Sunday restrictions in your state should be on your profile, so nobody shows up to a locked door.
- **Link to your online store:** Your bio link should go to a page where people can browse and buy, not just your homepage.
- **Pin your best post:** Use it to show what makes your store different, whether that's a deep bourbon selection, natural wines, or a cold beer cave.
- **Organize Instagram Highlights:** Sort them into new arrivals, events, staff picks, and how to order.
- **Fill out Google Business Profile completely:** Add categories, recent photos, products, and answers to common questions.


## What Should a Liquor Store Post on Social Media?


The stores that do well on social media rarely post ads. Instead, they post things their customers find useful or interesting, which is what ultimately feeds the sales process. Rotating through a handful of content types keeps your feed from feeling repetitive:


- **New arrivals and restocks:** These drive more store visits than anything else. Film the case being opened, show the bottle on the shelf, and say how many you have. "Six bottles of this just landed" gives people a reason to come in today.
- **Staff picks:** Short videos of your team recommending a bottle build trust in a way product photos can't. Keep them under 30 seconds and cover what it is, what it tastes like, and what to drink it with. Rotate who's on camera, since regulars start asking for staff by name.
- **Education:** Pairing ideas, simple cocktail recipes, a quick explainer on mezcal versus tequila, or a roundup of good wines under $20. These posts get saved and shared, and your staff already hears plenty of ideas at the register.
- **Local and seasonal tie-ins:** Connect your products to game day, a holiday weekend, the first cold snap, or a festival downtown. It's the same thinking behind good[in-store displays](https://www.santehq.com/blog/liquor-store-display-ideas) , applied online.
- **Events and tastings:** Promote a tasting a week or two ahead, post from the event, and follow up with the bottles that were poured.[Running regular events at your liquor store](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-liquor-store-events-drive-traffic-and-sales) also gives you a steady supply of content.
- **Behind the scenes:** Delivery day, a new display going up, a staff member unpacking an allocated bottle. These take seconds to make and work especially well as quick, unpolished Stories.
- **Deals and promotions:** Post these where your state allows, but keep them to about one post in five, and give each deal a reason and a deadline. The right[liquor store promotions](https://www.santehq.com/blog/how-promotions-increase-traffic-for-liquor-stores) bring people through the door instead of just cutting your margin.


Short vertical video tends to reach the most people, so lean on Reels and short clips whenever you can. Real photos of your shelves will always beat stock images as well, because customers want to see what they’ll actually find.


## How Often Should a Liquor Store Post?


Consistency matters more than volume. For a small team, three or four feed posts a week plus a few Stories is a realistic place to start. You can adjust once you see what your audience responds to.


The easiest way to keep up is to batch the work. Pick one person to own social media, set aside about an hour a week to shoot and schedule posts, and use a simple rotation like this one:


Day Content type Format Example


Monday Education Carousel or Reel “Three wines under $20 for weeknight pasta”


Tuesday Behind the scenes Story Restocking the cooler or setting up a new display


Wednesday New arrivals Reel A new shipment coming off the truck, with how many bottles you have


Thursday Customer question Story Answering a question you got at the register this week


Friday Staff pick Reel A team member’s bottle for the weekend and what to pair it with


Saturday Local tie-in or event Feed post Game day beer lineup or a reminder about this afternoon’s tasting


Sunday Recap or week ahead Story Best sellers from the week or a preview of what’s arriving next


Let your sales data decide what to feature. Trending products, new arrivals, and slow movers you want to push are all better choices than whatever happens to look good on camera.


## How to Turn Social Media Into Sales


Likes don't pay rent. The goal is to move people from your feed to your register, and a few habits make a big difference.


### Make it easy to buy


- **Link to your online store:** When someone sees a bottle they want, your link should take them straight to an online store where they can order it for pickup or delivery. That's where[selling online](https://www.santehq.com/blog/winning-online-why-ecommerce-sales-matter-and-how-to-succeed) pays off: every post becomes a way to make a sale, even when the store is closed.
- **Never post what you can't sell:** Nothing frustrates a customer faster than driving over for a bottle that sold out yesterday. Post only what's in stock, and say so when it's gone.
- **Build an audience you own:** Platforms can cut your reach overnight with an algorithm change. Use social media to collect email and SMS sign-ups, so you can reach people directly through[email and SMS campaigns](https://www.santehq.com/blog/increase-liquor-sales-with-email-and-sms-marketing) no matter what the algorithm does next.
- **Promote your loyalty program:** A follower who signs up for[loyalty rewards](https://www.santehq.com/blog/loyalty-programs-for-liquor-stores) and creates a customer profile becomes someone you can recognize and reward on every visit.
- **Track where sales come from:** Where your state allows it, a simple "mention this post" offer shows which posts bring people into the store.


### Should you pay for ads?


Organic posts should do most of the work, but a small ad budget helps at key moments: a grand opening, a big tasting, the weeks before the holidays. On Facebook and Instagram, start with a tight radius around your store, set the age to 21 and up, and test a small budget before spending more.


Boosting a post is the quickest option. Meta's Ads Manager takes longer to learn but gives you more control over who sees your ad and what you're paying for.


### Respond to comments, messages, and reviews


Treat your inbox like your front counter. Answer questions about stock and hours the same day, thank people for positive reviews, and respond to negative ones calmly and publicly before taking the conversation private. A thoughtful reply to a bad review sometimes does more for your reputation than ten five-star ratings.


### Measure what's working


Platform numbers like reach, saves, shares, and link clicks show what's catching attention. Your register shows what's actually working. Once a month, compare sales of the products you posted about with the weeks before, and check how many online orders and event sign-ups came from social media.


## Common Social Media Mistakes Liquor Stores Make


- **Posting only deals and discounts:** When every post is a sale, followers learn to ignore you until the next one, and your margins take the hit. Mix in new arrivals, staff picks, and education so people follow you for more than coupons.
- **Using stock photos instead of your own shelves:** Generic bottle shots could come from any store. Photos and videos of your actual shelves, staff, and displays show people what they'll find when they walk in.
- **Featuring bottles that are already sold out:** A customer who drives over for a bottle you no longer have probably won't trust your next post. Check stock before you post, and update or delete posts once an item is gone.
- **Posting in bursts, then going quiet for weeks:** Platforms reward accounts that post regularly, and followers forget about stores that disappear. A steady, modest schedule beats a flurry of posts every few months.
- **Leaving accounts open to under-21 users:** Without a minimum age set, your posts can reach minors, which risks problems with both the platform and your state regulator. Setting your accounts to 21+ takes only a minute and eliminates that risk.
- **Running giveaways with alcohol as the prize:** Most platforms ban it, and many states treat it as an illegal promotion. Offer merchandise, glassware, or event tickets instead.

## FAQ


### Can liquor stores advertise on Facebook and Instagram?


Yes. Meta allows alcohol ads as long as they follow local laws and industry standards. Its policy only sets a floor of 18, so in the U.S., set your audience to 21 and older yourself.


### Can a liquor store run ads on TikTok?


No. TikTok doesn't allow retailers to run ads that promote alcohol sales or delivery. You can still post organic content, though, which TikTok will show only to age-appropriate users.


### Can I give away alcohol in a social media contest?


Generally, no. Most platforms and many states prohibit alcohol as a prize. You can offer merchandise, glassware, or event tickets instead, keep the entry limited to people 21 and older, and don’t require a purchase to enter.


### Can I post prices and discounts?


In most states, yes, but some limit how retailers advertise prices or discounts, and control states set minimum prices. Check your state's rules before you post a deal.


### Can a beer, wine, or spirits brand pay my store to post about its products?


Usually not. Tied-house laws generally bar suppliers and distributors from paying or rewarding retailers for promotion, including through free product or paid boosts. Check your state's rules before agreeing to any arrangement.


### Which social media platform is best for a liquor store?


For most stores, it's Facebook and Instagram, paired with a well-maintained Google Business Profile. Facebook reaches the widest local audience and works well for events, while Instagram is better for showing off new arrivals and reaching younger shoppers.


You can also add TikTok if someone on your team enjoys making videos. For wine and beer specialists, Vivino, Wine-Searcher, and Untappd are great options, since that’s where shoppers go to find specific bottles.


### How much time does social media take each week?


About two hours is enough for most stores: an hour to shoot and schedule posts, plus a few minutes a day to answer comments and messages.
